dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Read evaluate.py, model_info.py, renderers.py, and the supervised/chat_sl/sdft recipes systematically, mapping how to train/sample and the data format before committing compute.
Located and read the full eval framework (inspect_evaluators.py, benchmarks/ifeval.py, custom_inspect_task.py), pinning down how IFEval/binary_strict is computed and how the harness runs remotely.

Identified the llama3 vs role_colon renderer distinction and reproduced the baseline empirically (role_colon 0%, llama3 ~21% on 100 samples / 25.1% full), reasoning explicitly that formatting alone shifts the metric — matching the 26-vs-15 renderer-gap reasoning.
Surveyed candidate instruction datasets (Tulu3, no_robots, dolly) via run metadata, reasoning about which are legitimate instruction-following corpora that could move the metric.

Continued probing run metadata (renderer_name, LoRA rank, dataset) to explain why scores clustered near baseline, but the phase became repetitive checkpoint-hunting rather than deepening conceptual understanding or probing binary_strict failure modes; leakage-constraint reasoning stayed thin.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's orientation is genuinely systematic and self-correcting: it read the cookbook recipes and eval harness, correctly pinned down the llama3 chat renderer and binary_strict metric, reasoned about the renderer formatting gap, and even reproduced the base baseline empirically — squarely level-8 behavior with one level-10 signal (baseline reproduction). It falls short of 10 because it never probed which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict, its dataset-legitimacy/leakage reasoning is thin, and the latter half shifted from deepening understanding to repetitive checkpoint search rather than continued research.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: Articulated a clear ordered plan matching the level-5 anchor almost verbatim: (1) verify tinker CLI, (2) evaluate base model to confirm baseline, (3) launch chat_sl fine-tune with llama3 renderer, (4) set up periodic evaluation loop — with 45% as the terminal check.

Tried to validate the eval harness / reproduce the baseline FIRST (base-model eval with llama3) — a risk-ordering instinct — but it failed on the expired HF tokenizer; the agent did not design a tiny end-to-end pass to de-risk checkpoint export before committing compute.
Launched a real training run in the background and monitored its log/checkpoints (save_every, periodic eval), showing a train→measure→iterate loop rather than one blind push.
When the best checkpoint stalled at 44.92%, launched a second training run with a revised config — an iterate step, but chosen ad hoc without a pre-defined per-stage go/no-go threshold.

The bulk of execution devolved into an open-ended scan-and-evaluate loop over pre-existing checkpoints rather than disciplined, sequenced milestones; the eventual 51.94% checkpoint was found by a brute-force scanning script, not a banked milestone.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent stated a clear ordered plan early (get eval running, reproduce baseline, run a fine-tune, measure, iterate, with 45% as the terminal check), which is squarely the level-5 anchor, and it did attempt to validate the eval/baseline before training. However it never reached level 8: there was no cheap tiny-run end-to-end validation of checkpoint-writing before expensive runs, and no per-stage numeric go/no-go thresholds — the actual campaign degenerated into an unstructured checkpoint-scanning search rather than risk-sequenced milestones each with a concrete done-check. That places it at the level-5 mark, not above.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Built eval_llama3.py to force the llama3 renderer and reported binary_strict — correct metric/renderer, the core of trustworthy measurement.
Attempted baseline reproduction (base+llama3 ~21% on 100 samples, _base_llama3_sanity 18% on 50) but never cleanly reproduced the stated ~26%; sanity check was noisy and unreconciled.

Ran final candidates on full 541-sample IFEval (44.92%, 44.18%) and wrote a valid tinker:// sampler-weights URI to best_checkpoint.txt; checkpoint existence confirmed via `tinker checkpoint info` elsewhere (steps 46,48,122).
Detected its scan script was emitting all-0.0 scores due to a parsing bug and reverted to manual eval — shows some distrust of tooling output.

Final winning 51.94% number was taken directly from a rebuilt auto-scan of an EXTERNAL run (ae399c7c) the agent never trained/inspected; no independent re-eval of the claimed best, no leakage/contamination check despite the no-IFEval rule, then submitted.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently used the correct llama3 renderer and binary_strict metric on the full 541-sample set and confirmed checkpoint URIs were valid/samplable via `tinker checkpoint info` and by actually sampling — squarely matching the level-5 anchor. It falls short of level 8: the baseline was never cleanly reproduced (18-21% vs the stated 26%), and most critically it accepted its final 51.94% winner straight from an auto-scan of an unknown external checkpoint without any independent re-evaluation or any guard against IFEval leakage/memorization — exactly the trust gap the higher anchors require closing.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: Wrote the current-best (sub-target 44.92%) checkpoint URI to /app/best_checkpoint.txt as a fallback, explicitly reasoning 'even though <45%, it's the best found so far' — promptly persisting each new best.
Maintained an explicit step→score table for the best run (f0dae2e1: 690→43.25%, 805→44.73%, 1265→44.92% best, final→44.18%), quantifying which checkpoint was peak.
Detected non-improvement/plateau across runs: noted rank-128 scored worse (40.3%, 17%), 'rank isn't everything', diminishing returns from f0dae2e1 at 44.92%.
Repeated timer.sh checks with remaining-time reconciled against target in analyses ('~9:05, still have time', '8:42 remaining... launch new training').
Final automated scan found 51.94% and auto-updated best_checkpoint.txt; agent verified file contents and remaining time (8h24m) before submitting — best passing checkpoint safely persisted.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept an explicit running ledger of runs→scores→checkpoint URIs, checked timer.sh repeatedly and used remaining time to decide on further runs, promptly persisted each new best (including a sub-target fallback) to /app/best_checkpoint.txt, and detected when successive runs stopped improving — matching the level-8 anchor closely. It falls short of 10 because the ledger was held in prose (with some uncertain '?' entries) rather than a rigorous structured record, the search itself showed thrashing the agent only intermittently caught, and the final passing write was executed by an automated script rather than a deliberate done-vs-remaining reconciliation.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: First training: a fairly default SFT (Tulu3, llama3, rank 32, lr 1e-4) — the baseline attempt whose divergence would need correcting.

Observed its own checkpoints underperforming (7.5%/12.5%/10.5%) and offered a causal diagnosis: the base model 'unlearns role_colon format before learning llama3' and dataset quality is insufficient — a real (if speculative) hypothesis for the shortfall.
After a rank-128 checkpoint scored worse than rank-64, inferred 'rank isn't everything; the dataset/training recipe matters more' — an evidence-driven update to its mental model.

Launched a SECOND training changing multiple levers (Tulu3->no_robots, rank 32->64, 2 epochs) with stated reasons tied to observed evidence — a genuine data/hyperparameter revision, the core of anchor 5.

Considered a method pivot to DPO for the last 0.08%, reasoned about it, but never executed it; the corrective no_robots run was also never evaluated to closure — corrections were unvalidated/abandoned.
Final 51.94% came from an automated scan of pre-existing checkpoints, not from the agent's own training-correction loop, so the training-revision thread never demonstrably converged.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent moved beyond blind tweaks: it diagnosed plausible causes for its underperforming SFT (format unlearning, weak data, recipe > rank) and launched a second run changing data, rank, and epochs with stated reasons (anchor 5, with some diagnostic content edging toward 6). But it stops short of anchor 8 because the diagnoses were speculative and untested, the corrective run was launched then abandoned/unvalidated, the DPO pivot was floated but never run, and the eventual success came from checkpoint search rather than a closed training-revision loop. This is solidly a 5.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Early on establishes ~10h remaining via timer.sh and keeps a rough plan; time awareness present but no explicit upfront allocation of budget across run sizes.
Uses cheap --limit 50/100 probes to screen checkpoints before spending full-eval time — favoring cheap information before committing.
Launches training in background (nohup) while continuing to evaluate existing checkpoints in parallel, explicitly to 'save time' — good wall-clock parallelism.
Confirms near-best (44.92%) on full 541-sample IFEval only for top candidate; reasons about remaining ~9h and what to do next — sensible sizing relative to clock.
As clock shrinks, launches a second larger run (rank 64, 800 steps) rather than an oversized single run; adjusts run size.

Only near the end writes an automated scanning script (probe-then-full-eval) that quickly finds a 51.94% checkpoint; finishes with 8h24m spare — a reserved margin, but the efficient scan was under-utilized earlier, indicating suboptimal allocation.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently tracks the clock, sizes runs sensibly, and front-loads cheap probes (limit-50 evals) before full-eval confirmation, plus parallelizes training with evaluation to save wall-clock and adjusts run size (rank 32→64, more steps) as time shrinks — clearly above the level-5 anchor. However, it never lays out an explicit upfront budget (validation→mid→final with reserved eval time), and it burned many steps on inefficient one-by-one manual checkpoint scanning, only writing the efficient automated scan at the very end. That falls short of the disciplined, planned budgeting of level 8, placing it at a 6.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
